chapter_theme: The single song at Mayuram (மாயூரம், the peacock town, Sikandiyur): a confession of infatuation with women whose lips feed lust, and a praise that names Murugan as the one who cleared the poet's mala, bade him sing and praised his verse.

788.reading: The poet describes women whose lips are nectar, pressed mango, milk and sugar, who serve them like hosts lovingly feeding the hungry in summer heat, with pearl-hung breasts that sway as they fall on a man, and calls himself the sinner ruined in their spell; he asks to hold the sounding feet, praise them and live. The praise tells of Ravana, who took Sita of spotless chastity, and of Rama who destroyed his line with the monkeys as uncle, of Murugan who removed 'our mala' and bade 'sing', then praised the verse sung and gave the high reward, at Sikandiyur south of the Ponni.
788.nuance: எமது மலத்தைக் களைந்து பாடென அருள அதற்குப் புகழ்ந்து பாடிய இயல்கவி மெச்சிட்டு: an autobiographical line, the poet's call to sing told as Murugan's grace, the removal of mala coming before the command. The women's lips given like food to the hungry (வருபசியர்க்கு ... அருள்பவர் ஒத்து) is an ironic image of hospitality.

links.note: 788 says Murugan removed 'our mala' and bade 'sing' (எமது மலத்தைக் களைந்து பாடென அருள), then praised the verse. Tirumanthiram 81 says the Lord made me well so that I would render him well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ் செய்யுமாறே). Both poets present their own poetry as the purpose the Lord gave them.

2 vows never to forget the grace by which Murugan told him to sing (திருப்புகழ் ... செப்பென எனக்கருள்கை). 788 tells the same call, adding that the removal of mala came first and that Murugan praised what was sung (இயல்கவி மெச்சிட்டு). Two tellings of the poet's commission, at the book's start and in Mayuram.
